title: First chair
lede: Michele De Lucchi’s chair for Memphis: a metal hoop that carries a blue disc and two black balls.
summary: De Lucchi’s 1983 chair: tubular hoop, round seat, blue disc back, ball armrests.

source.label: National Gallery of Victoria: First, chair (D75-1985)

creator.name: Michele De Lucchi (designer); Memphis, Milan (manufacturer and retailer)

evidence.note: Downloaded the museum’s published image (694 × 859 px) from [the National Gallery of Victoria](https://www.ngv.vic.gov.au/explore/collection/work/20878/) to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue. The Met record was also read; it has no online image.

styles.note: Made and sold by Memphis; the Met calls it characteristic of the collective’s designs.

context: The NGV lists De Lucchi as designer and Memphis, Milan, as manufacturer and retailer; lacquered metal and wood, 90.3 × 66.2 × 46.2 cm, purchased in 1985. [NGV record](https://www.ngv.vic.gov.au/explore/collection/work/20878/).

The Met describes a black wooden seat disc on four tubular legs, with a tilted tubular hoop that carries a turquoise disc backrest and two black ball armrests. It calls the chair characteristic of the Memphis collective that De Lucchi co-founded with Sottsass. [Met record](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/753976), accession 2021.54.10.
observed: A gray tubular ring rises from the front legs and tilts back behind the seat.
A flat blue disc is fixed at the top of the ring as the backrest.
Two glossy black spheres sit on the ring at the sides as armrests.
The round seat is black, on four thin straight gray legs.
interpretation: The chair is drawn with lines and dots: a circle, a disc, and two balls. It shows that Memphis could be sparse. Here the play comes from geometry and a few colors, not from pattern.
borrow: Compose with a thin circular line and a few solid dots placed on it.
Let one saturated disc of color act as the focal point against black and gray.

rights.statement: The NGV allows its image to be downloaded for publications and non-commercial use and states that it believes the work to be in the public domain. The design is by a living designer and dates from 1983, so the catalogue treats it as in copyright and stores no image.
